clinicalPearls: AML is a clonal neoplasm characterized by infiltration of blood, bone marrow, and other tissues by proliferative, poorly differentiated myeloid cells (myeloblasts); historically the diagnosis required a marrow or blood myeloid blast count of >=20%, though the 2022 WHO classification eliminated the blast-percent requirement for cases with specific defining genetic aberrations (Harrison 22e p.825, p.826).

Most cases are idiopathic; genome sequencing suggests the majority arise from a limited number of mutations that accumulate with age. AML is the most common acute leukemia in older patients (median age at diagnosis 69 years) and causes 62% of leukemic deaths; only ~32% of patients survive 5 years (Harrison 22e p.825).

Auer rods are abnormal rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules; they are NOT uniformly present, but when seen they establish AML (and exclude acute lymphocytic leukemia) with certainty. AML blasts show fine lacy chromatin with one or more nucleoli and primary (nonspecific) cytoplasmic granules (Harrison 22e p.829).

Presentation is usually nonspecific and gradual (sometimes abrupt), reflecting marrow failure: fatigue (frequent first symptom) and anemia, abnormal hemostasis/bleeding and easy bruising from thrombocytopenia, and fever +/- infection from neutropenia/leukocyte dysfunction. Fever is the initial symptom in ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e p.828).

Multiparameter flow cytometry helps distinguish AML from acute lymphoblastic leukemia and identify subtypes (e.g., myeloid antigens CD13/CD117 in minimally differentiated AML; platelet antigens CD41/CD61 in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia); it has only a supportive role for WHO subtyping given the paramount importance of genetics, and is increasingly used to measure measurable residual disease (MRD) (Harrison 22e p.827).

Cytogenetic/molecular testing at diagnosis provides the most important prognostic information and drives risk stratification (European LeukemiaNet 2022 categories: favorable, intermediate, adverse). All AML cells contain genetic mutations, most recurring; the majority of patients now have a genetic lesion that can be specifically targeted (Harrison 22e p.826, p.827).

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), defined by t(15;17)(q22;q12) / PML-RARA fusion, is a distinct, highly curable subtype (~85% long-term survival) treated uniquely with tretinoin (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide; it is excluded from the ELN risk table and is a coagulopathy emergency (Harrison 22e p.826, p.833).

Myeloid sarcoma is a tumor mass of myeloid blasts at sites other than marrow (commonly skin, lymph node, GI tract, soft tissue, testis); it may precede or coincide with blood/marrow involvement, is associated with t(8;21), and patients with isolated myeloid sarcoma typically develop blood/marrow disease quickly and cannot be cured by local therapy alone (Harrison 22e p.828).

Infiltration of gingiva, skin, soft tissues, or meninges with leukemic blasts at diagnosis is characteristic of the monocytic subtypes and those with KMT2A chromosomal abnormalities; gum hypertrophy is a classic monocytic finding (Harrison 22e p.828, p.830).

Infectious complications during neutropenia are the major cause of morbidity and death during induction and postremission chemotherapy; fever develops in most patients but infection is documented in only about half of febrile patients, and empiric broad-spectrum antibacterial/antifungal therapy at onset of neutropenic fever has substantially reduced infectious deaths (Harrison 22e p.832).
harrison.pathophysiology: AML results from clonal proliferation of poorly differentiated myeloid progenitor (blast) cells that infiltrate the marrow, blood, and tissues, crowding out normal hematopoiesis and producing pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia/leukocyte dysfunction, thrombocytopenia). Leukemogenesis is driven by accumulating somatic mutations; clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), most often involving epigenetic regulators DNMT3A, TET2, and ASXL1, carries a ~10-fold increased risk of hematologic malignancy, though additional 'hits' are required to progress to leukemia. Recurrent genetic lesions define disease biology and presentation: fusion genes (e.g., PML-RARA from t[15;17]; RUNX1-RUNX1T1 from t[8;21]; CBFB-MYH11 from inv[16]/t[16;16] core-binding-factor AML; MLLT3-KMT2A; DEK-NUP214) and gene mutations (NPM1, present in ~30% of AML and ~60% of cytogenetically normal AML; FLT3, activating ITD or TKD mutations in ~30%; CEBPA; TP53; IDH1/IDH2 producing the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate that disrupts epigenetic processes). KMT2A rearrangements and monocytic differentiation favor extramedullary/tissue infiltration; t(15;17) APL drives DIC.
additionalDifferentials: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) - distinguished by flow cytometry/immunophenotype; presence of Auer rods confirms AML and excludes ALL
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) - may precede/evolve into AML; AML-MR is defined by antecedent MDS or MDS/MPN and/or specific cytogenetic/molecular features
Myeloproliferative neoplasm (including chronic myeloid leukemia) - antecedent hematologic disorder that can transform to AML
Therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML - after alkylating agents (4-6 yr latency) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (1-3 yr latency)
nonInfectiousMimics: Aplastic anemia / marrow failure syndromes (also present with pancytopenia)
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g., CML in blast crisis)
additionalInvestigations: CBC with manual differential (anemia normocytic normochromic; median presenting WBC ~15,000/uL; platelets <100,000/uL in ~75%)
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, and molecular studies (cornerstone of diagnosis and classification)
Cytogenetics and molecular testing at diagnosis (NPM1, FLT3-ITD/TKD, CEBPA bZIP, TP53, IDH1/IDH2, RUNX1, ASXL1 and others) for ELN risk stratification
Peripheral blood smear for blasts and Auer rods; peroxidase staining
Chemistry including uric acid, LDH, phosphorus, calcium, creatinine/BUN (tumor lysis screen); ~50% have mild-moderate uric acid elevation
Coagulation studies - PT, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer (screen for DIC, especially APL)
Cryopreservation of viable leukemia cells for future testing
HLA typing for potential allogeneic HCT; echocardiogram/MUGA for cardiac function; chest radiograph
Infection screen including SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses in patients with respiratory symptoms before chemotherapy
Measurable residual disease (MRD) assessment by flow cytometry or quantitative RT-PCR (e.g., NPM1, RUNX1-RUNX1T1, CBFB-MYH11, PML-RARA transcripts)
redFlags: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, t[15;17]/PML-RARA): coagulopathy/DIC emergency - presents with DIC-associated hemorrhage (may include significant GI, intrapulmonary, or intracranial bleeding); requires immediate recognition and ATRA-based therapy
Disseminated intravascular coagulation - classically in APL but also in monocytic AML and with extreme leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia; note thrombosis is also a recognized feature of DIC in APL
Hyperleukocytosis (WBC >100,000/uL, seen in ~20% at presentation) with pulmonary leukostasis and early CNS bleeding - associated with poor outcomes
Intracranial hemorrhage / CNS bleed - headache, vision changes, nonfocal neurologic abnormalities
Febrile neutropenia - fever in a neutropenic patient mandates immediate evaluation and empiric broad-spectrum antibacterials covering gram-negative organisms

Tumor lysis syndrome / uric acid nephropathy - hyperuricemia (aggravated by initiating chemotherapy); allopurinol/hydration started at diagnosis, rasburicase for severe cases (avoid in G6PD deficiency)

APL differentiation syndrome - within first 3 weeks of ATRA (or less commonly ATO): fever, fluid retention, dyspnea, chest pain, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural/pericardial effusions, hypoxemia; ~10% mortality if unrecognized
harrison.prognosis: Untreated AML is uniformly fatal; overall only ~32% of US patients survive 5 years. Cytogenetic/molecular risk is the dominant prognostic determinant: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), t(8;21) and inv(16) (core-binding-factor AML) a good prognosis (~55% cured), cytogenetically normal AML an intermediate outcome (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3), or monosomy 7 confer adverse risk with very poor outcomes and virtually no cure without transplantation. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favorable; in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation is favorable; FLT3-ITD carries negative prognostic impact. Clinical adverse factors include advancing age (the most important clinical factor), poor performance status, high presenting leukocyte count, antecedent hematologic disorder (MDS/MPN) or prolonged preceding cytopenias, and therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML. Achievement of complete remission (CR) and MRD-negative status predict longer survival.
pitfalls: Auer rods are not uniformly present in AML, so their absence does NOT exclude AML; their presence, however, confirms AML over ALL

Diagnosis based on blast percent alone is outdated - cases with defining genetic abnormalities (e.g., t[15;17], t[8;21], inv[16], KMT2A rearrangement, NPM1 mutation) qualify as AML even with <20% blasts; genetic/cytogenetic testing is mandatory for precise diagnosis

APL must be recognized urgently - delay or treating it like ordinary AML risks fatal DIC; high-risk APL (WBC >10,000/uL) requires immediate cytoreduction because ATRA can precipitate life-threatening differentiation syndrome and rapidly rising leukocyte count
Even infirm older patients generally benefit from treatment over supportive care alone - age and comorbidity should not automatically exclude therapy

Even patients with undetectable MRD remain at risk for relapse; without postremission therapy virtually all CR patients eventually relapse, and there is no consensus on the optimal MRD technique or its use to direct therapy
NPM1 prognostic favorability is negated by co-existing FLT3-ITD; prognostic mutations are not mutually exclusive (>80% of patients carry two or more)
Anemia at diagnosis is usually present but not typically severe and is normocytic normochromic - a 'mild' blood count abnormality can still herald AML
harrison.severityClassification: Risk stratification per 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) by genetics at diagnosis (APL excluded): Favorable - t(8;21)/RUNX1-RUNX1T1, inv(16) or t(16;16)/CBFB-MYH11, mutated NPM1 without FLT3-ITD, in-frame bZIP-mutated CEBPA. Intermediate - mutated NPM1 with FLT3-ITD, wild-type NPM1 with FLT3-ITD (without adverse lesions), t(9;11)/MLLT3-KMT2A, and abnormalities not classified as favorable or adverse. Adverse - t(6;9)/DEK-NUP214, KMT2A rearrangements, t(9;22)/BCR-ABL1, inv(3)/t(3;3) MECOM(EVI1), -5/del(5q), -7, -17/abn(17p), complex or monosomal karyotype, mutated ASXL1/BCOR/EZH2/RUNX1/SF3B1/SRSF2/STAG2/U2AF1/ZRSR2, and mutated TP53 (>=10% VAF). Classification (2022 WHO): AML with defining genetic abnormalities versus AML defined by differentiation; the >=20% blast requirement is removed for cases with specific defining genetic aberrations.
